_note: Fiscal figures are approximate structural balances — recurring revenue minus recurring spending, excluding one-time measures. All states are legally required to pass balanced budgets; 'deficit' here means structural imbalance papered over with reserves, one-time funds, or federal windfalls. Verify all figures against Pew Charitable Trusts Fiscal 50 (fiscal50.pewtrusts.org) and NASBO State Expenditure Reports before updating. Legislative control as of January 2026; 2025 state elections may affect NJ and VA entries.
source: Pew Charitable Trusts Fiscal 50 · NASBO State Expenditure Reports · Ballotpedia · state IFO equivalents

transferableLessons.title: Constitutional spending cap
transferableLessons.description: Limits how fast appropriations can grow — typically tied to population + inflation or personal income growth. Prevents the structural mismatch from compounding silently in years when revenue grows slower than spending. PA could adopt this by statute without a constitutional amendment.

transferableLessons.title: Supermajority to access reserves
transferableLessons.description: Texas requires a 2/3 legislative vote to withdraw from its rainy day fund. The high bar makes election-year drawdowns politically costly. PA currently requires only a simple majority, and the 'unexpected shortfall' language is contested — a supermajority rule would be the cleaner fix.

transferableLessons.title: Formula-driven reserve deposits
transferableLessons.description: Virginia's Revenue Stabilization Fund automatically deposits money when revenues spike above forecast and withdraws only when economic conditions deteriorate. Removes the political discretion that lets structural deficits accumulate quietly in good years.
